pages.text: Two nights before the exam, Vincent’s phone buzzed. A message from an unknown number read: “Real questions and answers for tomorrow’s paper. Only GH¢50. Pay now and get everything.” His heart thumped. He had not finished revising Mathematics, and the English comprehension still frightened him. He stared at the message. “Fifty cedis,” he whispered. “Nobody would know.”

He stared at the message.
“Fifty cedis,” he whispered.
“Nobody would know.”
pages.alt: A boy stares at a phone showing a message with a price, a lamp lighting his face.

pages.text: He thought about it all night. What if the answers were real? What if he passed easily? Then he thought of other questions. How could a stranger have the real paper? What if the message was a trick to take his money? And what if the examiners found out? The next morning he told no one. He kept the message and did not reply, and the worry sat in his stomach like a stone.

pages.text: At home, Vincent’s mother noticed that he was quiet. “What is it?” she asked, putting down her tape measure. He showed her the message. She read it, and she did not shout. “Thank you for telling me,” she said. “I understand the fear. But think. Who sells the answers to an exam? A person who either does not have them, or who has taken them dishonestly. Either way, you cannot trust them.”

pages.alt: A seamstress sits beside her son at a sewing machine, reading his phone.

pages.text: The next day, Vincent went to Mr Kotey. The form master listened carefully. “Many students get messages like this,” he said. “Some are scams that take your money and send nothing. If answers really do leak, examining bodies treat it as a serious offence. A student who is caught can have results cancelled, and the penalty can follow them. And even if nobody catches you, you have not learned the work.”

And even if nobody catches you, you have not learned the work.”
pages.alt: A teacher speaks seriously to a student at his desk with past papers stacked beside him.

pages.text: “There are other reasons too,” said Mr Kotey. “It is unfair to the student who studied for months. It teaches you to take shortcuts when life gets hard. And it hurts the reputation of every honest student in your school, because employers and universities start to doubt the results.” He paused. “Faith traditions and our national values all ask us to be honest. Notice that none of these reasons depends on being scared of a cane.”

pages.text: Then Mr Kotey did something better than lecture. “Let us make a plan,” he said. “Past papers from the last five years, an hour of Mathematics tonight, an hour of English tomorrow, and sleep. You have forty-eight hours, and that is enough to improve.” He added, “And let us report that message to the school, so the head teacher can warn others.”

pages.alt: A teacher and student write a two-day revision plan beside a stack of past papers.

pages.text: Vincent passed the exam with results he was proud of. He wrote to his younger brother, Felix, with his address and the date at the top. “House 2, Lagoon Road, Takoradi. 30th August, 2027. Dear Felix, I hope you are keeping well. Next year you will sit your exams, so I want to share some advice. Prepare early, practise past questions and ask your teachers for help. If anyone offers you answers, refuse and tell an adult. Honest results are worth more than stolen ones. Your loving brother, Vincent.”

“House 2, Lagoon Road, Takoradi.
30th August, 2027.
Dear Felix, I hope you are keeping well.
Next year you will sit your exams, so I want to share some advice.
Prepare early, practise past questions and ask your teachers for help.
If anyone offers you answers, refuse and tell an adult.
Honest results are worth more than stolen ones.
Your loving brother, Vincent.”
pages.alt: A boy writes a letter to his younger brother with his exam results folded beside him.

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: Vincent’s advice letter gave clear steps and reasons in full sentences. Notice that he wrote “refuse and tell an adult” and not “no way lol”. Advice letters often use commands such as “prepare”, “practise” and “ask”. Polite, direct language is clear and kind. The end.
